elements.element: Customer has no minimum purchase commitment.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 expressly permits a minimum purchase commitment if stated in an Order Form. Section 12.3's statement that Customer made no minimum-volume commitment conflicts with, and does not eliminate, that operative possibility.

elements.element: Fees are payable only for Services actually ordered or used.
elements.evidence: The word “otherwise” carves minimum-commitment shortfall true-ups out of the ordered-or-used limitation, allowing fees for Services not actually ordered or used.

elements.element: Any minimum purchase commitment is limited to the current 12-month term.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 states that any minimum purchase commitment “applies only to the current twelve-month term.”

elements.element: Customer may reduce any minimum purchase commitment on 30 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 permits the commitment to be reduced by Customer on thirty days' written notice.

elements.element: Any shortfall is resolved through a true-up.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 provides that any shortfall is settled by a true-up at the Order Form unit rates.

elements.element: The true-up is not a penalty.
elements.evidence: Section 2.1 expressly states that the true-up “is not a penalty.”

result.reason: The redline fully implements the fallback but not the preferred position because it still permits an Order Form minimum commitment and associated charges for unused or unordered volume. It goes beyond what is needed for the fallback by adding an Order Form amount limitation and an “otherwise” usage-based fee rule. It also leaves a direct inconsistency between Section 2.1's permitted minimum commitment and Section 12.3's acknowledgment that Customer made no minimum-volume commitment.
